bet.text: Maximum throughput from a self-sufficient, aggressively simple scorer with a hopper, instead of a passer that relies on its alliance partners.

demand.text: Two weeks into the competition season the team put throughput first and valued being self-sufficient, because elevating partners had not been enough against strong scoring robots. It judged that winning auto is not vital but that what the robot does in auto is. It also wanted a hopper, to resist defense in a hub-scoring role.

auto.text: Point-to-point paths are built for two center sweeps: under the trench on the way out to preserve odometry, over the bump on the way back, where relocalizing is easier.
A rotation turns the camera to the back hub tags before the bump, to recover from center-line collisions.

cycle.text: The intake fills the hopper and sensors preload the feeder. With a valid tag seen and tolerances met, the feeder runs and the intake retracts to compress fuel toward the shooter. In passing mode it aims at the closest corner of the alliance zone.

endgame.text: The binder describes no climber; in its extracted text, 'Climb' falls in the no-design-effort list, whose table columns were lost.

fallback.text: A failsafe mode fires from set positions with preset flywheel speeds and hood angles, without vision. The tag requirement can be overridden by hand, and the wheels can lock in an X under defense.

gave_up.text: The team set aside its 'Familiar' and 'Lightweight' objectives.
The rebuild skipped prototyping, and driver practice was quite limited before the district championship.
Localization was its biggest weak spot and limit at Champs, a member says.
An outside list notes a small hopper and no net.
A commentator says 4065's defense held it to essentially one hopper in a finals 2 shift.

changed.text: Blitz, a passer with two side four-bar intakes, a serpentine path and no hopper, was limited by intake and shoot-on-the-move speed.
The team's interview and posts date the rebuild decision to after the first event; its blog speaks of the first two competitions.
One post says Blitz's four-bar broke every match; another says its polycarbonate failed once and that breaking deploy chains were the biggest fault.

outcome.text: 53-23-0 in official play; won the Newton division; championship finalist; captain of the Newton alliance on Einstein; ranked 2 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 408.46, Newton).

solves.text: Stay fast and robust, with a smooth underside that does not get stuck on fuel

facts.text: 27.5 x 27 in chassis, modified from Blitz with the modules rotated 90 degrees
MK5n modules with R1 gearing, the lowest ratio, to minimize current draw
Four Kraken X60 drive, four X44 steer
Custom lowering blocks and a polycarbonate bellypan keep fuel from getting under the robot and stop it getting stuck
Chassis of 7075 punched box tube, which allowed 1/16 in walls
For Champs, skid plates went under the drivebase and the bumpers were raised to cross the bump
Outside plates on the sides bring the length by width to 27.5 by 27.75 in, for packaging of the intake deploy; wrapped with a string the perimeter is just under 110 in

cost.text: The bumper height was copied from Blitz for convenience, and the bump was forgotten in the heat of rebuilding

solves.text: Withstand impacts by strength; a powered bottom roller was added so that it could intake at maximum robot speed

facts.text: Takes up to this many at once
Deployed by one Kraken X60 with a #35 chain final reduction
Deploy gear ratio
One 2 in main roller and two 1.25 in lower dead-axle rollers, on two Kraken X60
Billet side plates about 0.6 in thick, split in two sections joined by five bolts each
A 2 x 2 box-tube 'bash bar' sits over the main roller to protect it
A championship interview calls it a four-bar once; the binder says a slap-down replaced the four-bar
The deploy went from 90:1 to 40:1 between the district championship and Champs, to move faster with less push force
The side plates were never meant to be this thick: it was the only aluminum in stock. They react to Blitz's intake, which kept breaking
Powered lower rollers make no huge difference for scattered fuel but noticeably speed up collecting from dense clumps; a broken pulley let the team try them fixed, which worked
The intake's hard stop is the bumper

cost.text: The team says it massively overdesigned it to make sure that it would not break
At first the lower rollers had printed hubs and polycarbonate tubes; a broken drive pulley was one reason for aluminum rollers with sprocket hubs and chain

The team broke basically everything except the side plates in the week before the district championship; for Champs the bash bar got 1/8 in walls, and during Champs, a member believes, the lower roller, which kept getting dented, got a thicker wall

solves.text: Resist defense and separate scoring from driving and shooting on the move

facts.text: Stows above the shooter and slides out on bearings when the intake deploys
Catchers lock it out so that it cannot be pushed back into the shooter
Capacity given in the team's championship interview (captioned), about
An outside list says just over 50 balls
Light-tinted panels show how much fuel is inside; sheet metal brackets with flush nuts let damaged panels be replaced easily
Each catcher is a one-way latch held up by rubber bands; the pair stop the crossbar on top of the hopper from sliding back
A large chamfer removes a corner the intake could not sweep, where fuel would fall out
A Teflon sheet on most of the ceiling is really important: without it fuel jams and lifts the hopper as the intake retracts

cost.text: An outside list says the hopper is small for a dumper, so the robot must cycle extremely quickly
Over-stuffed, it lifted at the intake side and a few times caused trouble under the trench; the driver came through at a slight angle or chamfer first

solves.text: Raise throughput over the serpentine path, which moved fuel needlessly before the shot

facts.text: Incline
Ten 1.25 in rollers and an indexing roller with nine 2.25 in 35A compliant wheels, four balls wide
All chained together at 1:1 on four Kraken X60
Teflon-covered backing boards in the tower and hopper improved consistency and throughput, the team says
A front backing board slides balls into the shooter more quickly

At the district championship floor and tower were separate powertrains; running the tower faster made balls slow down in the shooter at many ranges and hurt accuracy, so both ended at one speed. For Champs they were joined, to be simpler and more efficient
The front backing board, carbon fiber with Teflon tape, is what took throughput past 30 balls per second
The main limit was how quickly and consistently balls went from hopper to tower; gear ratios and blocker panels were tried, logs read, and what did not help was taken off after one or two hoppers
Rollers are aluminum with 1/32 in walls and printed shims; polycarbonate ones with 1/16 in walls were too flexible
Custom 6061 dead-axle hubs carry a 12 tooth sprocket, or two, and a bearing; reused from Blitz, they fix every roller at the same speed
Where no tensioner fits, chain center distances get around 0.015 in extra
It runs on open-loop duty cycle, at the current limit most of the time it shoots; the ratio was the one with the highest surface speed when full of balls
The live-axle compliant wheels, copied from 6328, allow compression to be changed by spacing

solves.text: Fit more fuel into each hopper cycle

facts.text: When the hopper sensor trips, at around 80% full, the feeder runs until its own sensor trips, just before the flywheel
Adds two rows of four per hopper cycle
The hopper sensor was moved down during the season so it would trigger earlier

solves.text: Keep exit velocity consistent across many shots

facts.text: 4 in aluminum drum with 1.5 in hood rollers
Flywheel overdrive ratio
Sustained maximum over a full hopper, as the team states it
The interviewer and an outside list say about 35 balls/s
The final brass flywheel was balanced; the team says a less extreme overspeed would also work
Aluminum supports hold the backing plates with zip ties where feeder rollers once were; the rollers made consistency and throughput worse
Drum of 6063 aluminum with a 1/16 in wall, wrapped in DKL grip tape, at 1.67:1 reduction from four Kraken X60
The hood rollers turn twice as fast as the drum, for about 75 to 80% of its surface speed: the aim is the most ball speed that still leaves enough backspin to stabilize the shot
Compression is about 0.4 to 0.5 in through the feeder, to save power, and 0.8 to 0.9 in at the drum and hood, for consistent exit speed
Flywheel steps: a 6 in stainless disk just over 1 lb at 3.44:1, then at 6.7:1, then 1.65 lb of brass with its pulley cut in and no spokes, because spokes dragged on the air
Going from the stainless to the brass flywheel brought about 5% more accuracy; more angular momentum gave more consistent and longer shots on both robots
It stays near the speed for the current distance to the hub, capped at the farthest hub shot unless passing, because spinning up from rest takes the most current
The 10 tooth pulley and flywheel rarely pass 12,000 rpm, of about 20,000 possible
Dead axles through the hood keep its plates parallel, which stub axles do not

cost.text: Rollers used before the backing plates made exit velocity inconsistent and spread the shot
The stainless flywheel loosened on its shaft at the district championship and was glued for the last day
Spin-up current was a major contributor to overheating the main breaker; current limits changed at the district championship took spin-up from just over 1 s to just under 2 s
The belt wraps little of the hood pulleys, as a better route's belt could not be sourced; raising the hood into the trench could strip the upper pulley's teeth, though it still shot fairly well
Laser cutting warped the big 1/4 in 7075 side plates, which had to be bent straight before assembly

functions.name: Vision relocalization

solves.text: Keep the robot's position good enough to aim after collisions

functions.type: one front Limelight 4 measuring tag distance

facts.text: Distance comes from the pixel height of the tag, looked up in a table
Averaging the tag's height to its middle fixed distortion when the hub tags are seen at an angle
Tag distance resets odometry translation, which sets shot parameters and corrects the auto path
The robot may not shoot without a visible tag unless overridden
In auto it turned to the hub and paused before the bump, so the one Limelight could see a tag slowly enough for an accurate pose; that left no time for a third sweep
Off-season: a Jetson Orin with three ThriftyCams and software copied from 1868

cost.text: A member says that with more time the team would have put a lot of effort into more cameras, since localization was the biggest limit at Champs; interruptions in auto, above all on Einstein, kept it from relocalizing on the hub, so it failed to cross the bump

functions.name: Base Subsystems and state machine

solves.text: Program only the logic specific to each subsystem

functions.type: code templates with finite state machines

facts.text: Servo and roller parent classes generate motor interfaces and logging from IDs, ratios and limits
Bring-up to basic functionality took about (captioned)
A button pushes a wanted state to the superstructure, which passes wanted states to subsystems

functions.name: Pass-on-the-move
functions.type: pose extrapolation with a lookup table

facts.text: Pose is extrapolated forward by a time-of-flight constant, then a passing table and a rotation calculation give shooter speed and rotation

solves.text: Change speeds quickly without remaking gearbox plates

facts.text: All gearboxes accept multiple ratios, so speeds change without remaking plates
The floor and tower gearboxes took any mix of up to six motors, and equal roller spacing let the two powertrains be joined later

functions.name: Impact-resistant electronics
functions.type: soldered, shock-mounted electronics on a brainpan

facts.text: As few connectors as possible: wires are soldered, remaining connectors hot glued or zip tied, and the roboRIO and battery sit on printed TPU

cost.text: The battery comes out from below: the robot goes on its side and a plate is unscrewed, which is slower than from the top

The robot browned out in the last 10 seconds of a few district championship matches, which the team thinks its changes for Champs avoided; current limits were set mostly by trial, and stiffer competition fuel forced changes at events

decisions.because: the strategy was mostly right but Blitz could not execute it well enough, and it was so integrated that iterations were very constrained
decisions.cost: about three weeks: 7 days of CAD (5 were allotted), 10 of fabrication, then bring-up, tuning and fixes until the district championship

decisions.choice: Aggressively simple design drawn from 254, 1678 and 6328
decisions.because: the timeline was extreme and those architectures had already proven themselves by Week 2
decisions.cost: an architecture that was not familiar to the team

decisions.because: it is simpler, more robust and a style the team knew it could make work, taking impacts by strength; the four-bar's failures had no obvious fix
decisions.instead_of: a four-bar that collapses on impact

decisions.because: two did not raise throughput, complicated the robot and constrained iteration
it makes the robot more defense resistant and separates scoring from shooting on the move
decisions.instead_of: using the alliance and neutral zones as the hopper

decisions.choice: Widen the shooter and feeder to four balls

decisions.because: chain has less rolling resistance, which made the system more power-efficient, and its small sprockets package better now that strong motors need large belt pulleys
decisions.cost: on Blitz, chain skipped in several places until tensioning was added

decisions.choice: Backing plates in the shooter tower
decisions.because: more rollers did not help balls per second and made exit velocity inconsistent
the team tried MegaTag and calls it reliable, but says its simple solution works very well
it was discussed on day 1 and judged beyond the team's experience and design resources that season, per one member's post
the lowest ratio minimizes current draw
at the design start few teams had nets; later a net's effect on trench crossing and on intake retraction was an unknown, and refining what it had promised more

decisions.choice: Flat polycarbonate with bent sheet metal brackets
decisions.because: the team doubted it could bend polycarbonate precisely enough, and it would likely crack at the bend after hits
the same mass gives more inertia at a larger diameter and higher speed; a heavier drum would need much more weight for the same effect

decisions.choice: Practice the trench shot against a defense robot
decisions.because: weeks of match simulation and defense practice before Champs taught when to use it and how to reach it under defense
